paras: The attempted lynching of John Keller and William Coulter took place on the night of Saturday, 18 November 1882, when a mob surrounded the jail at Taylorville, Christian County, Illinois, where the two men were held. The men had been arrested for the alleged criminal assault of a 16-year-old girl at Pana, and the mob had not taken them at last report. Papers outside the state tied the case to other Christian County crimes, and two predicted a lynching to come.

According to a dispatch from Pana, a girl of 16 named in most copies as Lena Zinn missed her railroad connection there while travelling from Mattoon to Beardstown. While she waited at the depot about 6 o'clock, Keller and Coulter were said to have enticed her away, one "representing himself to her as an officer, and the other as a hotel runner." The dispatch charged that they took her to an outhouse on the East schoolhouse grounds and assaulted her.
Keller, Coulter and a companion, Wm. Craiger, who said he had only followed them, were arrested. A later item added that the girl found her way back to the station before the arrests.

The only account of the mob appeared in the Ottawa Free Trader, which reported that on Saturday night the Taylorville jail holding the three men "was surrounded by a drunken and surging mob determined to Lynch the ravishers." At last accounts the mob had not done so, and the paper gave no size for the crowd, no names and no account of how it dispersed.

In early December a crime digest reported that a grand jury "at Pana" had indicted William Coulter and John Keller, their names printed as "Coulle" and "Kellar." No report of a trial or verdict was found.

The Pana dispatch ran from 17 November in papers from Illinois to St. Paul, Wheeling and Yankton under headlines such as "TWO BRUTES" and "DASTARDLY ASSAULT," treating the accusation as fact and naming no one's race. The Ottawa Free Trader reprinted it under "ANOTHER CHRISTIAN COUNTY HORROR" and added the attack on the jail without comment, calling the prisoners "the ravishers."

The Mineral Point Tribune in Wisconsin linked the case to the assault on Emma Bond and to an earlier Taylorville mob that had "partly lynched" two other prisoners, and said it would not be surprising if the next lynching "would prove more effective." In New Mexico the Lincoln County Leader predicted that the accused men's "necks will not stretch far enough to ever reach a trial."

Dispatches printed on 17 and 18 November placed the assault on the evening of 16 November, while a copy dated Pana, 18 November and the Ottawa Free Trader's "Friday evening of last week" point to 17 November.

bases: A mob surrounded the Taylorville jail intending to lynch the men held for an assault at Pana but had not done so at last report, an attempted lynching with no one reported killed (A7).

A 'drunken and surging mob' surrounded the jail to lynch the accused in an alleged rape case, an illegal group action under a pretext of justice, but no one was reported killed (A7); later items report an indictment, not a death (A10, A11).
The arrests and accusation are carried by several wire versions (A1, A2, A3, A5), but the jail mob itself appears only in the Ottawa Free Trader (A7).

accounts.label: Ottawa Free Trader
accounts.gist: Retold the wire story and added that on Saturday night a drunken mob surrounded the Taylorville jail to lynch the men, without success at last accounts.

accounts.label: Later notices
accounts.gist: Brief items said the girl found her way back to the station, that the grand jury indicted Coulter and Keller, and that the men might not live to reach trial.

framing.detail: Wire versions ran under crime headlines such as 'TWO BRUTES', 'DASTARDLY ASSAULT' and 'ANOTHER OUTRAGE', treating the accusation as fact and naming no race.
The Ottawa Free Trader called the accused 'the ravishers' and reported the mob without comment under 'ANOTHER CHRISTIAN COUNTY HORROR'.

The Mineral Point Tribune expected a 'more effective' lynching and said the regular course of law did not meet 'the demands of the situation'; the Lincoln County Leader predicted the men's 'necks will not stretch far enough to ever reach a trial'.
